takedown of the American food production system, author Michael Pollan offered a stunning exposé of the havoc that corn caused on water, soil, taxpayers, rural economies, and public health. Really? Corn is a serious problem? Indigenous, peaceable, abundant corn? Twenty years after Pollan’s exposé the wreckage from cultivating and harvesting corn has gotten worse. So much worse that the environmental and health consequences of growing America’s super surplus of corn has become the top political issue this year in Iowa, the country’s largest corn producer. The hazards of corn-based ingredients in ultraprocessed food, moreover, are the targets of a petition to the Food and Drug Administration by David A. Kessler, the agency’s former director. It calls for the FDA to revoke the “generally recognized as safe” status of industrial processed refined carbohydrates, arguing they have not been independently tested but are linked to chronic metabolic diseases like obesity and diabetes. Kessler’s petition is tantamount to an indictment of corn-based industrial food chemistry that is wrecking the nation’s health. Until now the biggest knock on corn is its exorbitant multibillion-dollar annual cost to U.S. taxpayers. And that cost , almost $8 billion this year in price supports and subsidies for crop insurance , never really generated national outrage. Abundant corn, after all, reflected decades of deliberate production policy, capable plant science, and yeoman family farm muscle that fed America. It’s a homegrown crop engineered, subsidized, and mandated into dominance until it became the king of American grain. A Justifiable Critique It’s been a long time coming but the fresh distaste for corn is well deserved. Here’s why. Corn is an absurdly prolific water polluter .
